# ML Fundamentals \- Deep Dive

# From examples and simple numbers to models that work on new data

Designed for CS Project II students moving from an approved proposal into implementation and evaluation. No previous machine learning knowledge is assumed. Basic arithmetic is sufficient; the small calculation is explained step by step.

---

## Session Outline

The central idea: A model learns by adjusting internal numbers using examples. A useful model must then perform well on appropriate examples it has not practised on.

* Session 1 — Building the foundations (suggested 90 minutes): Lessons 1–6. Begin with rules and examples, follow one learning update, and distinguish learning from memorisation.  
* Session 2 — Making sound project decisions (suggested 90 minutes): Lessons 7–10, classroom activities, and the CS Project II checklist. Discuss model size, data, synthetic examples, and evaluation.

Learning outcomes: Explain how models learn; distinguish learning types, training, and inference; use validation appropriately; interpret a confusion matrix and QA metrics; assess model size, data quality, synthetic data, and bias; and justify whether a model meets a project’s needs.

Teaching note: All library rules, dataset sizes, scores, and numerical experiments below are invented teaching examples unless explicitly attributed to a source. They are not Strathmore University policies or measured research results. The diagrams are original explanatory illustrations. The animal pictures are AI-generated, photo-style illustrations for teaching, not photographs collected as research data.

## Our Two Running Examples

**Example 1 — Image classification:** A system receives one photograph and chooses between two labels: cat and dog. Begin with a single clearly visible animal. Later, examine poor lighting, unfamiliar animals, unusual backgrounds, and images containing neither class.

**Example 2 — Question answering (QA):** A system answers questions from a fictional library guide. Our first passage is: “The library closes at 8 p.m. on weekdays. Students may borrow three books.” The question “When does the library close on weekdays?” should produce “8 p.m.”

Important distinction: Classifying a photograph means selecting a category. Answering a question may mean selecting words from a passage or generating a response. These tasks share learning principles but need different outputs, training targets, and evaluation methods.

# Lesson 1: From Written Rules to Learning from Examples

## 1.1 What Does “Learning” Mean Here?

Imagine describing every possible cat to a programmer: ears, fur, eyes, tails, body shape, and every possible camera angle. A rule such as “pointed ears means cat” will fail for some dogs. The difficulty is not writing an if-statement; it is finding rules that handle the variety.

Machine learning uses examples to fit a rule or mathematical function. People still choose the task, data, model, and learning procedure. Training changes parts of the function so its predictions better match a chosen objective. The computer does not need human-like awareness to do this.

Image example: Rather than manually describe every ear shape, provide many photographs with reliable cat/dog labels. A model can learn combinations of visual patterns associated with each label.

QA example: A fixed lookup can answer an exact stored question. A learned system may handle “What time does it shut?” as well as “When does it close?” It must still receive suitable evidence or have relevant learned information; flexible wording does not guarantee factual correctness.

![][image8]

*Figure 1\. Handwritten rules and learning from examples. Both approaches require human decisions; the learned approach fits parameters from data. The handwritten rules shown are deliberately simplistic.*

## 1.2 Where Do AI, ML, and Deep Learning Fit?

Artificial intelligence (AI) is a broad area concerned with computer systems performing tasks associated with intelligent behaviour. Machine learning (ML) is one approach within AI. Deep learning is a branch of ML using neural networks with multiple processing layers. Not all ML uses deep learning: linear models and decision trees are useful examples.

Generative AI describes systems that produce content, such as text or images. It describes a kind of capability, rather than a separate size category. A cat/dog classifier normally selects a label; a generative image model creates an image.

## 1.3 Types of Learning: Where Does the Feedback Come From?

A useful question is: what tells the model that it should change? The answer helps distinguish the main learning approaches. “Supervised” does not mean a teacher watches every calculation. It means training examples supply desired outputs (Google, n.d.-a).

## Supervised learning — learn from examples with answers

Think of practice questions with a marking guide. Each input has a target: the answer the model should produce. For images, a person checks each photograph and labels it cat or dog. For our library QA system, an example contains a passage, a question, and a verified answer such as “8 p.m.” The model predicts, compares with the target, and adjusts.

Classification predicts a category, such as cat or dog. Regression predicts a numerical quantity, such as an animal’s weight in kilograms. Both can use supervised learning. Generating a written answer is another kind of output; it is not automatically a simple classification problem.

## Unsupervised learning — look for structure without supplied answers

Think of sorting a mixed box of photographs without labels. A clustering method groups examples that look similar according to its chosen representation. It might group photographs by animal shape, but it could instead group them by background or colour. People must inspect what the groups mean; cluster 1 is not automatically “cats.”

For the library, clustering unlabelled questions might reveal groups about opening hours, borrowing, and membership. This helps organise questions or identify common needs. It does not, on its own, teach the system the correct answers. “No answer labels” does not mean “no human choices”: people still select the data, representation, and method.

## Semi-supervised learning — use a few labelled examples and many unlabelled ones

Imagine 200 checked cat/dog photographs and 5,000 photographs without labels. A method can learn from the checked examples and use information in the others. One approach assigns tentative model-generated labels, called pseudo-labels, to selected unlabelled examples. These labels can be wrong and must not be treated as verified truth.

For QA, a small set of checked passage–question–answer examples can be combined with unlabelled library text or questions using a suitable training method. Merely adding unanswered questions to a folder is not semi-supervised learning. The training procedure must actually use the unlabelled material.

## Self-supervised learning — make a practice target from the data itself

Think of covering part of a sentence and trying to recover it. In “The library closes at eight \_\_\_,” the original text supplies “p.m.” as the target. A next-token model similarly learns to predict the following token from earlier ones. No person needs to write a separate answer label for every position.

For images, one approach hides patches of a photograph and trains a model to reconstruct them. These practice tasks can help learn useful representations. A model that reconstructs photographs is not automatically a reliable cat/dog classifier, just as predicting words does not guarantee correct library answers. Further task training or suitable prompting and evaluation may be needed.

Semi-supervised and self-supervised are related ideas, but the names answer different questions: semi-supervised describes a mixture of labelled and unlabelled data; self-supervised describes how targets are created. A system can use both across its training stages.

## Reinforcement learning — learn actions from rewards

Think of learning a game: an agent acts, observes what happens, and receives a reward. It tries to improve its decisions to obtain greater total reward over time. A reward is a feedback score, not necessarily the correct answer for every step.

A library assistant could learn when to retrieve another passage, ask for clarification, or answer, using carefully designed feedback for supported, useful responses. An image-related example is an agent learning where to move a camera to obtain a clearer view before classification. A fixed cat/dog classifier is normally taught more directly with labelled images.

Reward design matters. Rewarding only fast replies might encourage guessing; rewarding only user approval may favour pleasing but unsupported answers. Human feedback does not always imply reinforcement learning: people can also label supervised examples or provide preferences for other training methods.

## How the approaches fit together

These are ways of learning, not competing model sizes. A QA model might use self-supervised pretraining, supervised fine-tuning on checked answers, and later reward-based training. Transfer learning means reusing previous learning for another task; fine-tuning describes further parameter training. Neither replaces the question of where the new feedback comes from.

Check your understanding: Labelled cats and dogs → supervised. Grouping unlabelled library questions → unsupervised. A few verified labels plus many unlabelled images → semi-supervised. Predicting a hidden word using the original sentence → self-supervised. Learning retrieval decisions from rewards → reinforcement learning.

A simple library opening-hours database lookup may still solve the task without ML. Choose the learning approach because it serves the problem, not because its name sounds advanced.

# Lesson 2: Inputs, Labels, Features, and Numbers

## 2.1 Start with One Example

An example is one case used for learning or evaluation. Its input is what the model receives. Its target is the desired output used during training or assessment. A dataset is a collection of examples. A prediction is what the model actually produces.

Image example: Input \= a photograph; target label \= cat; prediction \= dog. The target and prediction are different things. A wrong label can teach the wrong association even when the training software works correctly.

QA example: Input \= the library passage plus a question; target \= the correct answer or its location in the passage. The target is not normally handed to the model as part of its input. Doing so would give away the answer.

## 2.2 What Does the Computer Receive?

An image is stored as numbers. A small greyscale image has one brightness value per pixel; a common colour image has red, green, and blue values. A 100 × 100 colour image therefore contains 30,000 channel values before any additional processing. These are input values, not 30,000 learned parameters.

Text is divided into tokens: pieces that may be words, parts of words, or punctuation. A tokenizer assigns token IDs. Those IDs are looked up or transformed into numerical vectors called embeddings. A larger token ID does not mean a more important word. Token boundaries depend on the tokenizer.

![][image9]

*Figure 2\. Images and text reach models as numbers. Input values and learned parameters have different roles. Token IDs are illustrative; both the passage and question must be represented for the QA model.*

A feature is information used to make a prediction. In a simple system, people might define features such as average brightness. Neural networks can learn intermediate features from pixels or token representations. Features are useful only if they help with the real task.

Important caution: Resizing, normalising, and tokenising must be consistent between training and use. Any preprocessing that learns statistics, such as a mean or vocabulary fitted for an experiment, must be fitted on training data rather than the held-out test set.

Check your understanding: Are 1,000 photographs the same as 1,000 pixels? No. The first counts examples; the second counts elements within image inputs.

# Lesson 3: What Is Inside a Model?

## 3.1 Think of Adjustable Numbers

A useful starting picture is a machine with adjustable dials. Its structure determines how inputs are processed. Its parameters are the internal numbers adjusted during learning. In a neural network, many parameters are weights and biases. A weight controls how strongly an input contributes; a bias can shift the result.

A tiny mathematical model could compute: score \= weight × input \+ bias. A larger model combines many operations. A neural-network unit combines values and usually applies a nonlinear function; layers connect these units. Nonlinearity helps represent relationships that repeated straight-line operations alone cannot express.

Architecture means the arrangement of the model’s operations. A training algorithm describes how parameters are fitted. A trained model combines an architecture with its fitted parameter values. A saved checkpoint records a training state that can be loaded again.

## 3.2 Parameters Are Not Settings Chosen in the Same Way

Parameters are learned during training. Hyperparameters guide the process or define the model: examples include learning rate, batch size, layer count, and training limits. Students choose or tune hyperparameters using training and validation results. They do not use final test performance as a repeated tuning signal.

Image example: A visual model may learn patterns useful for distinguishing ears, fur, and shapes, but it can also learn misleading background patterns. A convolutional neural network processes local image regions using shared filters; other architectures, including vision transformers, are also possible.

QA example: A text model combines information about the question and passage. Transformer attention lets one position use information from other positions. In our library example, useful relationships include “when,” “closes,” “weekdays,” and “8 p.m.” Attention is a computation, not proof of human understanding.

Check your understanding: If two models have the same architecture, must they behave identically? No. Different data, training choices, or parameter values can produce different behaviour.

# Lesson 4: How a Model Learns — One Adjustment at a Time

## 4.1 The Learning Loop

For the supervised neural-network examples in this lesson, training repeatedly follows five steps: make predictions; compare them with targets; calculate a loss; calculate how parameter changes affect that loss; and update parameters. Other ML methods may learn through different procedures.

![][image10]

*Figure 3\. The training loop. The target is used to assess the prediction; the optimizer changes parameters using the calculated gradients.*

Loss is a numerical penalty for predictions that differ from the training target. The precise formula depends on the task. A gradient describes how loss changes as a parameter changes. Backpropagation calculates gradients through a neural network. An optimizer, such as gradient descent, uses them to update parameters. The learning rate helps control the size of an update.

## 4.2 A Tiny Worked Example

This deliberately simplified example demonstrates an update, not a real cat/dog classifier. Let x \= 1 represent one made-up image feature, let the target y \= 1 stand for cat, and let the model produce a raw score s \= w × x. There is no bias in this example. A raw score is not a probability.

Start with weight w \= 0.2. The prediction is s \= 0.2 × 1 \= 0.2. Use squared-error loss: L \= (s − y)². The loss is (0.2 − 1)² \= 0.64.

For this formula, the gradient with respect to w is 2(s − y)x. Therefore, the gradient is 2 × (0.2 − 1\) × 1 \= −1.6. Students do not need to derive this formula here; it tells the optimizer which direction changes the loss.

Choose learning rate 0.1. Update rule: new weight \= old weight − learning rate × gradient. Thus, the new weight is 0.2 − 0.1 × (−1.6) \= 0.36.

Predict again: s \= 0.36. The new loss is (0.36 − 1)² \= 0.4096. The error on this example has decreased. One internal number changed; the model did not receive a new human-written rule.

Important caution: An improvement on one example does not establish a useful classifier. A real system must learn across many examples and be evaluated on new ones. Classification commonly uses a loss such as cross-entropy rather than this teaching example’s squared error.

## 4.3 Apply the Same Idea to Both Tasks

Image example: The model may assign a low probability to the correct class. A classification loss penalises this, and updates can increase the correct class probability. Confidence in a wrong answer can incur a larger penalty than a less confident wrong answer.

QA example: An extractive model can predict the start and end positions of “8 p.m.” in the passage. Training penalises incorrect positions. A generative QA model can instead learn to predict the next answer token from the question, passage, and preceding tokens. Predicting plausible words is not itself a guarantee of truth.

Activity — Try the next update: Using w \= 0.36, x \= 1, y \= 1, and learning rate 0.1, calculate the next weight. Suggested answer: gradient \= −1.28; new weight \= 0.488; new loss \= 0.262144.

Check your understanding: What actually learned? The parameter values changed according to the objective. The example does not demonstrate consciousness or perfect understanding.

# Lesson 5: Training and Inference Are Different

## 5.1 Practice Time and Use Time

Training changes parameters. Inference uses a trained model to produce an output. The same model can answer thousands of questions without changing its weights. Saving a chat history or retrieving a document does not, by itself, constitute parameter training.

Image example: During training, labelled photographs provide feedback. During inference, a new photograph enters and a class prediction leaves. The correct label may be unknown until a person checks it.

QA example: At inference time, the system receives the question and relevant passage. Giving it a revised passage that says “6 p.m.” can change its answer without any weight update. The context changed. The model was not necessarily retrained.

## 5.2 Batch, Step, and Epoch

A batch is a group of examples processed together. A training step commonly refers to one parameter update. An epoch is one pass through the training dataset. With 1,000 examples and batch size 100, one epoch contains 10 updates in a simple setup with one update per batch. Twenty epochs involve 200 updates and 20,000 example presentations, but still only 1,000 distinct examples.

Important caution: Gradient accumulation and other training arrangements can change the relationship between batches and optimizer steps. For large text corpora, training may be described using tokens and steps rather than complete epochs.

Repeated practice can help optimisation, but it does not create new independent evidence. Hours are also an unreliable comparison: the same work can take different times on different hardware.

Check your understanding: If a model uses a document in a prompt, has it necessarily learned that document permanently? No. It may simply be using information available in the current context.

# Lesson 6: Learning, Memorising, and Knowing When to Stop

## 6.1 Three Different Jobs for Data

Training set — practice material: used to fit parameters. Validation set — development check: used to compare settings, choose checkpoints, and decide when to stop. Test set — final assessment: reserved for evaluating the selected approach after development decisions are made.

An illustrative split is 700 training, 150 validation, and 150 test examples out of 1,000. This is not a mandatory ratio. The split must suit the task, available data, and the kind of future use being claimed. Small datasets may need carefully designed cross-validation and an independent final assessment where feasible.

![][image11]

*Figure 4\. Separate the data before training. Validation informs development; the final test set must not become repeated practice material.*

## 6.1.1 Validation and Evaluation: Related, but Different

Evaluation means measuring how well a model or system performs. Validation is evaluation during development to guide decisions. Final test evaluation estimates performance after those decisions are fixed. The same metric, such as accuracy, can be measured on training, validation, and test data; the data’s role is what changes.

Think of practice work, a mock exam, and a final exam. Training fits parameters using practice work. Validation helps choose how to prepare. The test provides a separate final assessment. Repeatedly using the final exam answers to change the model would undermine that assessment.

Image example: Train two candidate cat/dog models on the training set. Compare their validation results, including cat and dog errors, and select one. Fix the model and decision threshold before measuring its performance on the test images.

QA example: Use validation questions to choose a retrieval setting or an instruction that helps the system avoid unsupported answers. Then evaluate the chosen system on held-out questions, including questions whose answers are absent. Trying many prompts against the final test questions is still test-set tuning, even if no weights change.

A metric is a numerical summary of performance. Loss is the quantity used to guide training; the reported task metric may be different. Lower training loss does not automatically mean more correct answers on new data. Lesson 10 works through the task metrics.

Cross-validation is useful when development data is limited. For example, divide development data into five folds, train on four and validate on the fifth, then repeat until every fold has served as validation. Average the results and examine variation. Fit preprocessing separately within each training fold, and keep related animals, source documents, or paraphrases together. Cross-validation does not make leakage harmless or remove the need for an honest final assessment.

## 6.2 Underfitting, Useful Learning, and Overfitting

Underfitting means the model has not captured enough useful structure. Performance is poor even on training examples. Possible causes include an unsuitable model, weak inputs, difficult optimisation, or insufficient training.

Generalisation means performing usefully on appropriate unseen examples. Overfitting means fitting peculiarities of the training set that do not transfer well. A model can improve on training examples while getting worse on validation examples (Google, n.d.-b).

Image example: Every training cat appears on a sofa and every dog on grass. A model may exploit the background. Test it with cats on grass and dogs on sofas to reveal the shortcut.

QA example: Many training questions have the answer “8 p.m.” A model that repeats this answer can fail when the passage says “6 p.m.” or asks how many books a student may borrow. Test whether the answer follows the supplied evidence.

## 6.3 Why More Training Is Not Always Better

Consider these invented checkpoint results: epoch 2 — training loss 0.65, validation loss 0.68; epoch 5 — 0.40 and 0.45; epoch 10 — 0.20 and 0.30; epoch 20 — 0.05 and 0.50. Among these checkpoints, epoch 10 has the lowest validation loss even though epoch 20 has the lowest training loss.

![][image12]

*Figure 5\. An illustrative learning curve, not a measured experiment. The marked checkpoint is best among the displayed validation results; the final checkpoint is not automatically best.*

Early stopping monitors a chosen validation measure and stops when improvement has stalled for a specified patience period. Save the best checkpoint and restore it if that is the selection rule. A single noisy fluctuation need not trigger stopping. The measure may be validation loss or a task metric chosen in advance (TensorFlow, n.d.).

Important caution: Longer training is not inherently harmful. If validation performance is still improving, further training may help. Conversely, high training and validation errors do not prove that more epochs are the solution. Inspect data, labels, model suitability, learning rate, and the task definition.

Other responses to overfitting include obtaining more varied data, appropriate augmentation, simpler models, and regularisation. Regularisation discourages overly specific solutions; weight decay and dropout are examples. These methods need validation rather than automatic application.

## 6.4 Data Leakage: Accidentally Giving Away the Answers

Image leakage: Splitting photographs randomly may put near-identical frames of the same animal in both training and test sets. If the claim concerns new animals, group images by animal or capture session before splitting. Keep transformed copies of an image in the same partition as the original.

QA leakage: Paraphrases of the same question-answer pair can cross partitions. If the claim concerns unseen documents, split by document or source before generating questions. A claim about new questions over a fixed library collection may need a different design: state exactly what is unseen.

Use only the training partition to create training augmentations or synthetic examples. Never generate training material from held-out test answers. Repeatedly changing the model after inspecting test failures turns that test set into development data; acknowledge this and obtain a new independent evaluation when needed.

Activity — Choose and diagnose: Which displayed checkpoint would you select using validation loss? Epoch 10\. What if all test photographs are duplicates of training photographs? The reported result would not demonstrate generalisation to independent photographs.

# Lesson 7: Small, Large, Base, and Fine-Tuned Models

## 7.1 Model Size Is About Capacity, Not Just File Size

Parameter count is a common way to describe model size. A model with 10 million parameters has 10 million fitted numbers; one with 1 billion has 1,000 million. More parameters can support more complex patterns but do not guarantee better results for a particular task.

There is no universal boundary separating “small” and “large” across all ML. The terms depend on the model family and context. Architecture, training data, objective, and training quality all matter.

A larger parameter count usually increases storage and computing requirements under comparable conditions. Actual speed and memory also depend on hardware, numerical precision, input length, and architecture. Quantisation stores numbers with fewer bits; it can reduce storage without reducing parameter count.

Image example: A compact pretrained visual model may meet the project’s accuracy and phone-speed requirements. A larger model that gains little accuracy but cannot run on the intended device may be less suitable.

QA example: A smaller model with the correct library passage may answer the scoped question better than a larger model given no reliable source. This is a hypothesis to evaluate, not a promise that smaller models always win.

## 7.2 “Base” Has More Than One Meaning

Training-stage meaning: A base model often means a pretrained model before further task-specific or instruction-following adaptation. It can be small or large. A base language model may continue text fluently without reliably following a user’s instructions.

Family-size meaning: Some model families use “Base” as a named architecture size alongside “Small” or “Large.” Read the model documentation to determine which meaning applies. Do not infer capabilities from the name alone (Google, n.d.-a).

A baseline is different: it is a reference method used for comparison. It could be a majority-class predictor, keyword lookup, or an existing model. A “base model” is not automatically the right experimental baseline.

## 7.3 Different Ways to Build on Existing Work

* Training from scratch: Start without pretrained task knowledge in the parameters and fit a model using the available training process. This can be expensive for deep models; a small conventional ML model may still be practical.  
* Pretraining: Learn reusable patterns from a broad dataset before adapting to a downstream task. In text, self-supervised prediction is common.  
* Transfer learning: Reuse knowledge from a model trained for another setting. For image classification, a pretrained feature extractor can be paired with a new classifier.  
* Fine-tuning: Continue training some or all parameters using task-relevant data. Freezing layers means keeping those parameters unchanged while other parts learn.  
* Instruction tuning: A form of additional training using instructions and desired responses to improve instruction-following behaviour.  
* Prompting: Change the instructions or context supplied at inference time. Ordinary prompting does not update model weights.

![][image13]

*Figure 6\. Training changes parameters; inference uses them. Retrieval supplies external evidence at use time and does not itself train the answering model.*

## 7.4 Question Answering and Retrieval

Extractive QA selects an answer span from a passage. Generative QA writes an answer, potentially in different words. Both require suitable evaluation; neither is guaranteed correct merely because a passage is supplied (Hugging Face, n.d.-a).

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) first finds relevant material, then provides it to a generative model with the question. For the library example, retrieve the opening-hours paragraph before answering. If retrieval finds an outdated rule, the answer may be wrong despite fluent writing.

A useful diagnostic separates retrieval from answering: Did the correct passage reach the model? If yes, did it use the passage correctly? A retrieved document store and a model’s weights are different places where information can reside.

Check your understanding: Can a small model be a base model and later be fine-tuned? Yes. Size and training stage are different descriptions.

# Lesson 8: Dataset Size — How Much Is Enough?

## 8.1 Count Meaningful Variety

More relevant, varied, correctly labelled data can improve learning. More duplicated, irrelevant, or wrongly labelled data can waste resources or teach unwanted patterns. Dataset size should therefore be reported alongside what the examples represent.

Image example: Ten thousand frames from one short cat video do not represent ten thousand independent cats. A smaller collection covering different animals, cameras, backgrounds, and lighting may provide more useful variety. Whether it performs better must be tested.

QA example: Ten thousand paraphrases of one opening-hours question provide limited coverage. A useful collection also covers borrowing limits, exceptions, conditions, ambiguous questions, and questions the guide cannot answer.

For images, report image count, class count, and relevant independent groups such as animals or capture sessions. For text, report documents, question-answer pairs, and tokens where appropriate. File size in megabytes alone does not describe the learning content.

## 8.2 Quality, Coverage, and Balance

* Correctness: Are labels and answers trustworthy? Check disagreements and ambiguous examples rather than assuming all supplied labels are correct.  
* Relevance: Does the data resemble the intended use? Studio animal photographs may not represent blurry phone photographs.  
* Coverage: Are difficult cases and important user groups represented? QA data should include supported, unsupported, and ambiguous questions.  
* Balance: Do some classes or question types dominate? Preserve a realistic evaluation distribution while also reporting performance for important minority cases.  
* Independence: Are duplicates and closely related examples controlled? A large row count can conceal a small amount of independent information.

Important caution: Oversampling a minority class repeats evidence; it does not create new independent observations. Augmentation may introduce useful variation, but it cannot guarantee coverage of missing real-world conditions.

## 8.3 A Practical Way to Estimate Data Needs

Define the task and baseline first. Train with progressively larger subsets of the training data, keeping validation conditions comparable. Plot validation performance against training-set size. This is a data-size learning curve; it answers a different question from loss plotted against epochs.

If performance continues to improve, more suitable data may help. If it plateaus, investigate labels, coverage, model limitations, or the difficulty of the task. A plateau is evidence about the current setup, not proof that all further data are useless.

No universal number of images or QA pairs guarantees success. Data needs depend on task complexity, variation, model choice, pretraining, required reliability, and evaluation uncertainty. Choose a feasible pilot, inspect errors, and discuss the collection plan with the supervisor.

Check your understanding: Does training for 100 epochs turn 500 examples into 50,000 independent examples? No. It increases exposure to the existing examples.

# Lesson 9: Synthetic Data — Useful Examples or Repeated Mistakes?

## 9.1 What Counts as Synthetic Data?

Synthetic data are artificially created examples rather than direct observations of the intended real-world cases. They may come from a simulator, a rules-based generator, or another ML model. Synthetic does not automatically mean incorrect, independent, realistic, or private.

Data augmentation usually transforms an existing example: slightly crop a photograph, adjust brightness, or carefully paraphrase a question. A simulator can render a new scene with controlled lighting. A generative model can create an image or draft a question-answer pair. These methods are related, but their sources and risks differ.

Image example: A modest brightness adjustment can expose a classifier to useful variation. A crop that removes the animal makes the original label inappropriate. A generated “dog” image might contain unrealistic anatomy or a telltale texture that becomes a shortcut.

QA example: From “Students may borrow three books,” generate “How many books can a student borrow?” and verify the answer “three.” A generated answer of “five” is a wrong training target. A paraphrase that removes “on weekdays” from an opening-hours question may also change its meaning.

## 9.2 When Can It Help?

Synthetic examples can target a known gap, vary wording, simulate conditions that are expensive to capture, or provide practice for a specialised task. The benefit depends on realism, correctness, coverage, and the training mixture. Generating a large number of similar examples can leave the original gap unresolved.

Research example: Gunasekar et al. (2023) trained a coding language model using selected web material together with synthetic educational material. This demonstrates a useful application of synthetic data; it does not establish that every generated dataset will improve every task.

## 9.3 What Can Go Wrong?

* Inherited errors: A generating model can supply wrong labels, unsupported answers, stereotypes, or omissions. The learner may reproduce these patterns.  
* Limited diversity: Thousands of generated variations may repeat a narrow set of situations or writing styles.  
* Mismatch with reality: Artificial images or questions may be easier than real inputs, producing misleading development scores.  
* Contamination: Using test questions, test answers, or closely related material to generate training examples undermines independent evaluation.  
* Privacy assumptions: Generated data may reproduce sensitive details from its source. “Synthetic” is not proof of anonymisation or permission to use the material.

Model collapse describes degradation that can occur across generations when models learn from generated material and lose aspects of the original data distribution, including uncommon cases. Shumailov et al. (2024) studied recursive training and this loss of information. This is distinct from ordinary overfitting within one training run; it is not an inevitable outcome of every use of synthetic data.

## 9.4 A Practical Synthetic-Data Experiment

Begin with an independent real validation set and real test set. Identify a concrete weakness in the training data. Generate or transform examples only from permitted training sources. Check labels, factual support, diversity, duplicates, and unwanted artefacts. Record the generator, prompts or rules, filtering, and mixture proportions.

Compare a real-data baseline with one or more real-plus-synthetic mixtures under documented training budgets. Use validation results to choose a mixture. Evaluate the selected approach on the untouched real test set and inspect difficult cases. Where feasible, compare more real data and ordinary augmentation as alternatives.

Important caution: There is no universally correct real-to-synthetic ratio. If a larger mixture requires more training work, report that difference; otherwise, an apparent data benefit may partly reflect extra computation. Synthetic-only test results cannot establish performance on the real target population.

Activity — Audit a generated pair: Passage: “Three books may be borrowed.” Generated question: “How many books may be borrowed for two weeks?” Answer: “Three.” What is wrong? The question introduces a loan period that the passage never states. Repair the question or obtain supporting evidence.

# Lesson 10: What Makes a Model Good or Bad?

## 10.1 Good for Which Task, Users, and Conditions?

A good model meets a defined need with credible evidence. It performs usefully on independent examples, handles important cases, and fits practical constraints. A poor model may memorise, exploit shortcuts, fail on minority cases, invent answers, or be too slow or expensive for its purpose.

A model is not good merely because it is large, new, trained for many hours, or successful on a few demonstrations. Define acceptance criteria with the supervisor before selecting the final model. There is no single score that makes all models good.

## 10.2 Image Classification: Read the Confusion Matrix

Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that are correct. In an invented test set of 95 cats and 5 dogs, always predicting cat gives 95% accuracy but finds no dogs. A high overall score can therefore hide complete failure on an important class.

A confusion matrix is a count of actual labels against predicted labels. It shows which classes the model confuses. In the separate teaching example below, there are 100 images: 50 cats and 50 dogs. Each photograph contains one animal and receives one prediction.

Choose cat as the positive class and dog as the negative class. “Positive” is simply the class we are counting as the event of interest; it does not mean good, correct, or preferable. Here, “negative” means dog only because this example has exactly two classes.

Read the rows as the actual animal and the columns as the model’s prediction.

| Actual ↓ / Predicted → | Cat (positive) | Dog (negative) |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Cat: 50 actual | 40 True positives | 10 False negatives |
| Dog: 50 actual | 5 False positives | 45 True negatives |

True positive (TP): An actual cat is predicted as cat. The model found the chosen positive class correctly. There are 40\.

False negative (FN): An actual cat is predicted as dog. The model missed a cat. There are 10\.

False positive (FP): An actual dog is predicted as cat. The model raised a false “cat” result. There are 5\.

True negative (TN): An actual dog is predicted as dog. The model correctly rejected “cat.” There are 45\.

“True” or “false” says whether the prediction was correct. “Positive” or “negative” says what the model predicted. Read both words together. The correct cells lie on the diagonal; the other cells are errors. Software may reverse the axes, so always read the labels.

## 10.2.1 Turn the Counts into Useful Metrics

Accuracy — How often was the model correct overall? (TP \+ TN) ÷ all examples \= (40 \+ 45\) ÷ 100 \= 85%.

Precision for cat — When it said “cat,” how often was it right? TP ÷ (TP \+ FP) \= 40 ÷ 45 \= 88.9%. The denominator is predicted cats.

Recall for cat, also called sensitivity or true positive rate — Of all actual cats, how many did it find? TP ÷ (TP \+ FN) \= 40 ÷ 50 \= 80%. The denominator is actual cats.

Specificity, or true negative rate — Of all actual dogs, how many did it correctly call dog? TN ÷ (TN \+ FP) \= 45 ÷ 50 \= 90%.

False positive rate — Of all actual dogs, how many were wrongly called cat? FP ÷ (FP \+ TN) \= 5 ÷ 50 \= 10%. This is not the same as the fraction of predicted cats that are wrong.

False negative rate — Of all actual cats, how many were missed? FN ÷ (FN \+ TP) \= 10 ÷ 50 \= 20%. It is 1 − recall; false positive rate is 1 − specificity.

F1 score — A single summary balancing precision and recall through their harmonic mean. F1 \= 2TP ÷ (2TP \+ FP \+ FN) \= 80 ÷ 95 \= 84.2%. It is not their ordinary average and does not use true negatives.

Support — The number of actual examples of a class: 50 cats and 50 dogs here. Always report counts as well as percentages. Finding 4 of 5 cats and 400 of 500 cats both gives 80% recall, but the amount of evidence is very different.

Balanced accuracy — The average recall across classes. Here it is (80% \+ 90%) ÷ 2 \= 85%. In the earlier 95-cat/5-dog example, always predicting cat gives balanced accuracy of (100% \+ 0%) ÷ 2 \= 50%, exposing the failure hidden by 95% ordinary accuracy.

These definitions follow standard classification evaluation practice (scikit-learn developers, n.d.). If a denominator is zero, the metric may be undefined; explain the reporting convention rather than quietly interpreting it as reliable performance.

## 10.2.2 Which Mistake Matters, and Where Is the Cut-off?

Suppose a system sends predicted cat images to a cat-only catalogue. False positives add dogs to the catalogue, so precision matters. If the goal is to find as many cats as possible for later human review, missed cats are costly, so recall matters. Neither goal removes the need to report both types of error.

A threshold is the cut-off used to turn a score into a label. For example, predict cat when its score is at least 0.50. Lowering the cut-off generally produces more cat predictions: recall cannot decrease on a fixed scored dataset, but false positives can increase. Raising it generally reduces cat predictions and can miss more cats. Scores need not be well-calibrated probabilities.

Choose the threshold on validation data according to the task’s error costs, then fix it for the final test. There is no universally best 0.50 threshold or universally best F1 score.

For more than two classes, the matrix grows: three classes produce a 3 × 3 matrix. Compute each class’s precision, recall, and F1 by treating that class as positive and the others as negative. Macro-F1 averages class F1 scores equally; weighted-F1 weights them by support. A single average can still hide a weak class.

Inspect results by lighting, background, camera, and other relevant conditions. Also test inputs outside the intended classes: a forced cat/dog prediction on a car is not meaningful animal identification. Consider an appropriate rejection or human-review process.

## 10.3 Question Answering: Correct, Supported, and Useful

QA needs its own evaluation because an answer is often text rather than one of two labels. A cat/dog confusion matrix cannot by itself score every possible sentence.

Exact match (EM) checks whether a prediction matches an accepted reference answer after stated text-normalisation rules. If 16 of 20 held-out answers match, EM is 80%. Specify how case, punctuation, and alternative correct answers are handled. A valid paraphrase may still fail exact match.

Token-overlap F1 compares the words or tokens in a predicted answer with those in a reference. This is different from cat-classification F1: it counts shared answer tokens, not cats and dogs. Standard QA evaluators define their own normalisation and aggregation rules (Hugging Face, n.d.-b).

Worked example: Reference \= “three books”; prediction \= “books.” With simple whitespace tokenisation, one of the one predicted tokens is correct, giving precision 1/1 \= 100%. One of the two reference tokens was recovered, giving recall 1/2 \= 50%. F1 \= 2 × 1 × 0.5 ÷ (1 \+ 0.5) \= 66.7%, while exact match is 0\. The overlap score gives partial credit even though the answer misses the requested number.

Word overlap is not factual understanding. “The library does not close at 8 p.m.” overlaps strongly with “The library closes at 8 p.m.” but reverses the meaning. Evaluate generated answers with a clear human-review rubric as well.

For each question, record whether the answer is correct, supported by the passage, and complete without invented details. Separately check whether the system handles absent answers appropriately. For example, the weekday passage gives no Sunday hours: “The passage does not specify Sunday hours” is appropriate; inventing a Sunday closing time is not.

Report each rubric dimension separately. In an invented review of 20 answered questions, 17 factually correct answers gives correctness of 85%, while 15 fully supported answers gives evidence support of 75%. A statement can happen to be correct without being justified by the supplied passage. Define the scoring rules before reviewing and double-check disagreements.

## 10.3.1 A Confusion Matrix for the Decision to Answer

A useful separate binary task is deciding whether the supplied passage contains enough information to answer. Let positive mean answerable; the predicted positive means the system chooses to answer.

True positive: The answer is present and the system attempts an answer. False negative: The answer is present but the system abstains. False positive: The answer is absent but the system attempts an answer. True negative: The answer is absent and the system abstains.

For example, among 20 answerable and 10 unanswerable questions, suppose the system answers 18 of the first group and wrongly attempts 3 of the second. TP \= 18, FN \= 2, FP \= 3, TN \= 7\. Answerability precision is 18/21 \= 85.7%; recall is 18/20 \= 90%; correct abstention on unanswerable questions is 7/10 \= 70%.

This matrix evaluates the decision to answer, not answer correctness. An attempted answer to an answerable question can still be wrong. Evaluate the actual answers as well. Reporting only accuracy among answered questions can reward a system that avoids almost every question; also report coverage, the fraction it answers: 21/30 \= 70% here.

For RAG, first check retrieval: for example, on 20 questions with known supporting passages, did a sufficient passage appear among the top three retrieved results? If it did for 16, the retrieval hit rate at 3 is 80%. State this definition explicitly. Then assess the answers. This separates “the evidence was not found” from “the evidence was found but used badly.”

## 10.4 Confidence, Cost, and Reliability

A confidence score is not proof of correctness. Calibration concerns whether stated probabilities align with observed frequencies of correctness over comparable cases. A chatbot’s statement “I am 95% certain” is not automatically a calibrated probability.

Measure response time on the intended hardware, memory requirements, and operational cost where relevant. Compare models on the same evaluation examples and conditions. A small difference on a tiny test set may reflect sampling variation rather than a dependable improvement.

Run repeated training trials where feasible and report variability, not just the best run. Keep the dataset split, model version, settings, code version, and evaluation procedure traceable. After deployment, monitor for changed inputs or rules; useful performance can decline when conditions change.

Check your understanding: Can a model with lower overall accuracy still be preferable? Yes, if it better meets the agreed task requirements, such as detecting an important minority class or meeting a strict response-time constraint. Explain the trade-off with evidence.

## 10.5 Bias: One Word with Several Meanings

A bias is a systematic tendency, rather than a one-off mistake. In ML, the word has several meanings. Always say which one is intended.

A model’s bias parameter is an adjustable offset. In score \= weight × input \+ bias, a bias of 0.3 shifts the score by 0.3. This is a mathematical parameter, not evidence that the model treats people unfairly.

Inductive bias means the assumptions that help a learning method generalise. For example, an image model may be designed to reuse the same pattern detector across different parts of a photograph. Assumptions can be useful, but can fail when they do not fit the task.

Statistical bias refers to systematic error arising from simplifying assumptions. A model that is too restrictive may repeatedly miss a real pattern and underfit. Variance describes how much the fitted model changes with the training sample. These ideas connect to underfitting and overfitting, but they are not the same as social unfairness.

## 10.5.1 Bias in Data and in Real Use

Selection or coverage bias: The data leaves out important situations. If most training animals are photographed in bright light, the classifier may perform poorly on dark images. If library QA is trained only on formal English questions, it may struggle with everyday wording, spelling variation, or other intended languages.

Label or measurement bias: The recorded targets or measurements systematically misrepresent the task. A labeller who repeatedly calls small dogs “cats” teaches a wrong association. Outdated library answers teach yesterday’s rules even when the training code is correct.

Shortcut learning: The model relies on an easy but unreliable clue. Cats always on sofas and dogs always on grass can teach “sofa means cat.” A QA system may assume every “when” question is answered by “8 p.m.” without using the actual passage.

Social or harmful bias concerns patterns that produce unjust disadvantages or reinforce stereotypes about people. In a library service, systematic failure on questions from an intended language group could create unequal access. A performance gap should prompt investigation of data, design, and context; an overall score cannot establish fairness (Google, 2025).

Class imbalance is unequal class counts, such as 95 cats and 5 dogs. It can encourage majority-class predictions, but is not automatically proof of harmful bias. A balanced cat/dog dataset can still omit dark images, and a naturally imbalanced dataset may reflect real use. Examine coverage and error costs, not only counts.

## 10.5.2 How Students Can Investigate Bias

Start by identifying the users and conditions the project claims to serve. Check training coverage, label quality, and errors for those conditions. Compare class and subgroup metrics with their sample counts. For example, 90/100 correct bright images and 12/20 correct dark images gives 90% versus 60% accuracy; the smaller dark-image sample also carries more uncertainty.

For QA, compare supported-answer rates for formal and everyday phrasing of equivalent questions, while keeping related paraphrases in the same data split. Review whether failures come from retrieval, understanding the question, or generating the answer.

Respond to a diagnosed cause: collect missing examples, correct labels, improve retrieval, or revise the model and threshold. Re-evaluate on independent data. Balancing a dataset or adding synthetic examples does not automatically remove bias. Do not collect sensitive personal attributes without an appropriate justification and safeguards.

Check your understanding: Is every error bias? No. A single wrong cat prediction may be an isolated error. A repeated pattern of failure under a particular condition suggests a systematic problem worth investigating.

# Classroom Discussion and Project Application

## Activity: Choose the Better Model

Image scenario (invented): Model A has 99% training accuracy, 74% validation accuracy, and a 20 MB file. Model B has 92% training accuracy, 88% validation accuracy, and a 7 MB file. Both were evaluated on the same independent validation set. Which deserves further investigation?

Suggested response: B has better evidence of generalisation in this comparison and lower storage needs. A’s larger training–validation gap warrants investigation. Selection still requires class-level errors, evaluation uncertainty, target-device measurements, and final independent testing.

QA scenario (invented): A large model answers 18 of 20 familiar questions correctly but invents answers for 8 of 10 unanswerable questions. A smaller model with retrieved evidence answers 17 of the 20 correctly and appropriately abstains on 9 of the 10 unanswerable questions. Which is better for a library help service?

Suggested response: The smaller system may better meet a requirement to avoid unsupported answers, but the sample is too small for a broad claim. Expand evaluation and inspect retrieval, missed answers, latency, and costs. This compares complete systems, so the difference cannot be attributed to model size alone.

## Activity: Read the Errors, Then Choose an Action

Using the cat-positive matrix, explain why a dog labelled cat is a false positive. Then switch the positive class to dog. Suggested answer: That same error becomes a false negative for dog; the prediction has not changed, only the class being counted.

A QA system answers “8 p.m.” to every question. What should the evaluation include? Suggested answer: Varied answerable questions, unanswerable questions, evidence support, and answer correctness. A high score on repeated closing-time questions would be weak evidence.

## CS Project II: Evidence Students Should Prepare

* Problem and objective: State who needs the system and what measurable improvement is expected. Explain why ML is appropriate and identify a simpler baseline.  
* Data: Record provenance, permissions, collection method, labels, counts, independent groups, class balance, missing cases, and any synthetic-data process.  
* Split design: Explain what is held out, why it represents the intended claim, and how duplicates, related examples, preprocessing, and generated examples are controlled.  
* System analysis and design: Show the input-to-output pipeline, model role, data preparation, external services or retrieval, human decisions, and handling of failure cases.  
* Implementation: Record the architecture or pretrained model, version, parameter count where relevant, frozen/trainable parts, training settings, environment, and version-controlled code.  
* Experiments: Report the baseline, controlled comparisons, training and validation curves, checkpoint-selection rule, repeated-run variability where feasible, and computing budget.  
* Evaluation: Present task-appropriate metrics, test-set size and composition, representative errors, subgroup or difficult-case results, and practical performance.  
* Limitations and responsible use: Explain unsupported inputs, uncertainty, privacy, bias, and needed human oversight. Safety-critical applications require a much stronger validation and oversight plan than these classroom examples.  
* Supervisor review: Validate scope, dataset suitability, method, evaluation criteria, and readiness with the supervisor. Update the report alongside implementation.

Traceability example — Image project: Objective to classify new animal photographs → classifier feature → test on held-out animals → class-level metrics and error examples. QA project: Objective to answer questions from a guide → retrieval and answering features → held-out questions including unsupported cases → correctness, evidence support, and abstention results.

## Exit Questions

* What changes during neural-network training? The trainable parameter values.  
* Why can training loss decrease while validation loss increases? The model may be fitting patterns specific to the training examples.  
* Does “base” always mean small? No; it may describe training stage or a named architecture size.  
* Does a million generated examples guarantee improvement? No; correctness, diversity, relevance, contamination, and real-data evaluation matter.  
* What makes a model good? Evidence that it meets clearly defined requirements on appropriate independent data and within practical constraints.

# Quick Reference Glossary

Example: One input case, with a target where applicable. Dataset: A collection of examples. Label/target: The desired output. Feature: Information used for prediction. Prediction: The model’s output.

Parameter: An internal number fitted through training. Weight: A parameter controlling a contribution. Bias: An adjustable offset in a model; this meaning differs from social or dataset bias. Hyperparameter: A setting guiding model structure or training.

Loss: The numerical training penalty. Gradient: How loss changes with a parameter. Backpropagation: A method for computing gradients through a neural network. Optimizer: The rule that uses training information to update parameters. Learning rate: A setting influencing update size.

Batch: A group of examples processed together. Step: Usually one optimizer update. Epoch: One pass through a training dataset. Checkpoint: A saved model/training state. Inference: Producing outputs with a trained model.

Generalisation: Useful performance on appropriate unseen cases. Underfitting: Failure to capture enough useful structure. Overfitting: Fitting training-specific detail that does not transfer. Leakage: Information entering development that should have remained unavailable for independent assessment.

Token: A unit of text determined by a tokenizer. Embedding: A numerical vector representation. Pretraining: Broad initial learning for later reuse. Fine-tuning: Additional parameter training for adaptation. RAG: Retrieval of relevant material to support generated answers.

Synthetic data: Artificially created examples. Augmentation: Transformations of existing examples intended to preserve useful meaning. Baseline: A reference method for comparison. Calibration: Agreement between predicted probabilities and observed correctness frequencies.

Evaluation: Measurement of performance. Validation: Evaluation used to guide development. Confusion matrix: Counts of actual versus predicted classes. Precision: Correct positives among predicted positives. Recall: Positives found among actual positives. Specificity: Negatives correctly rejected. F1: Harmonic mean of precision and recall.

# **Build Phase – Development Sprints**

Dear Students,

The development phase will proceed through structured sprints and regular progress checks, alongside continued work on Chapter 5 and the earlier chapters.

A sprint is a defined period of focused project work with **clear tasks, deliverables and a progress review**. Each sprint should produce a demonstrable improvement in your project and evidence of what has been completed, tested and documented. These sprints apply to **all projects, regardless of project type**; the specific implementation and evaluation evidence should be appropriate to your approved objectives and methodology.

At the beginning of each sprint, agree on realistic priorities with your supervisor. At the end, be prepared to demonstrate your work, explain your decisions, discuss challenges and identify the next tasks. **Maintain your documentation alongside development** throughout this phase.

## **Sprint I: Data Preparation and Development Environment Setup**

The first sprint establishes a reliable foundation for implementation. This applies to **all projects, regardless of project type**. By the end of this sprint, I expect to see:

* A **properly configured development environment**, with the required tools, dependencies and configuration in place.  
* A **clean and professionally organised codebase**, with a clear folder structure and instructions for setting up and running the project.  
* All project code maintained using **Git version control**, with meaningful commits that show your development progress. Keep passwords, API keys and other sensitive information out of the repository.  
* Relevant data, databases, APIs, files, hardware or other **resources prepared and checked**, as applicable. For data-driven projects, document the data source, preparation steps and any access or ethical requirements.  
* **Appropriate use of automation** for repeatable setup, data preparation, testing or development management, where it supports your workflow.  
* **Corrections from earlier chapters completed**, with proposal-related content revised into project documentation and aligned with the system you are actually developing. Chapter 4 should reflect the analysis and design guiding your implementation.

**Use student access before paying for development tools.** Apply through [GitHub Education](https://github.com/education/students) using your academic email and the required enrolment evidence, then redeem the relevant [Student Developer Pack](https://education.github.com/pack) offers in your own accounts. Keep the verification, expiry dates and account recovery details available.

**Put the benefits to work.** Use GitHub Pro for private project collaboration, the included Codespaces allowance for a repeatable development environment, and eligible JetBrains student tools where useful. [GitHub Copilot Student](https://education.github.com/pack) can support coding and explanations within its current allowances; review and test its output. Monitor usage and stop unused development environments.

Be prepared to demonstrate that the project runs in your development environment, show the repository and prepared resources, and explain how this foundation supports the next stage of implementation.

## **Sprint II: Core Functionality, Integration and Initial Testing**

Due: next week, at the sprint progress review.

In this sprint, you will move from preparation to a working implementation of the core project functionality. Build on the foundation established in Sprint I and prioritise the features or technical components that directly address your approved objectives. By the end of this sprint, I expect to see:

* A clear set of sprint **tasks linked to your objectives**, showing what has been completed, what remains in progress and any issues affecting delivery. Validate the scope and priorities with your supervisor.  
* A **working core workflow** that can be demonstrated from input through processing to output. The implementation should perform a meaningful project task; screens, mock-ups or isolated components alone do not demonstrate completion of the core workflow.

Include relevant screenshots, outputs or test records, and update Chapter 4 diagrams where justified design changes have occurred.

## **AI-Assisted Research Workflow**

The diagram below illustrates the code, training and evidence cycle for AI/ML projects. Other projects should adapt the same principles of version control, repeatable testing and verified AI assistance to their own implementation.

![][image14]

*Fig 1: Sprint II — AI/ML development workflow.*

### **How to Work Through the Cycle**

**1\. Define the question and establish a baseline.** Begin with a specific question linked to an approved objective: what should improve, and how will improvement be measured? Implement a simple baseline and agree on suitable metrics, data splits and constraints with your supervisor before comparing alternatives.

**2\. Develop locally and version the work.** Keep application code, reusable training modules, notebooks and configuration in your laptop’s codebase. Ask the IDE agent to explain unfamiliar code and add useful comments about assumptions, design decisions and potential failure points. Review these comments for accuracy. Commit and push the tested changes to GitHub; keep credentials and sensitive data out of the repository.

**3\. Run a reproducible experiment in Colab.** Open the notebook from GitHub and load any supporting modules from the intended code version. Mount Google Drive in the Colab runtime and read the prepared datasets. Record the Git commit, dataset version, dependencies, parameters, random seeds and run identifier. **Fit preprocessing on training data only**; use validation data for development decisions and reserve the test set for final evaluation.

**4\. Preserve the evidence in Drive.** Save model checkpoints, preprocessing artefacts, configuration, metrics, plots, predictions and logs in a clearly named folder for each run. Include enough information to connect every output to its code and data versions. Save notebook edits back to GitHub so that the recorded code matches the experiment. Files left only in the temporary Colab runtime should not be treated as a permanent record.

**5\. Bring results back to the local IDE.** Use Google Drive for desktop to make the experiment folders available on your laptop, and confirm that synchronisation is complete before analysis. This local connection is separate from mounting Drive inside Colab. Give the AI agent the relevant code and readable outputs, such as metric files, logs and plots; access to a model file alone does not explain its performance.

**6\. Use the agent to investigate, then verify.** Ask it to compare the baseline and current run, identify error patterns, review code for leakage or implementation faults, and suggest a testable explanation. Require it to point to the actual files and results supporting each observation. **Treat its explanations as hypotheses**: check them against the code, data, experiment evidence and credible literature. Never turn an unverified AI statement or invented citation into a research finding.

**7\. Test an improvement and document the decision.** Make a controlled change, rerun the experiment under comparable conditions and record whether the evidence supports improvement. Preserve unsuccessful runs and explain limitations rather than reporting only favourable results. Review important decisions with your supervisor, then update Chapter 5 with the methods, verified results and your own interpretation. Record material AI assistance and follow applicable institutional disclosure requirements.

### **Example agent prompt**

“Review this notebook and the baseline and current-run results. Identify supported differences, possible data leakage and failure patterns. Refer to the exact code and output files, distinguish observations from hypotheses, and propose one controlled follow-up experiment. Do not invent results or references.”

At the Sprint II review, be prepared to show the versioned code, a reproducible baseline or core pipeline, saved experiment evidence, and one example of an AI suggestion that you checked. Explain what you accepted or rejected and why. **You remain responsible for understanding the code and defending the research conclusions**.

## **Sprint III: Project Completion, Deployment and Final Evaluation**

In this sprint, you will move from the working core demonstrated in Sprint II to a **complete, usable and evaluated project**. Complete the agreed functionality, refine the system around normal user tasks, deploy it in an appropriate environment, and finish the report and demonstration materials. The final solution should work coherently from the user’s first action to the intended outcome.

Begin by reviewing the remaining tasks and acceptance criteria with your supervisor. **Complete the approved objectives before adding optional features.** Any necessary scope adjustment must be agreed and reflected consistently in the implementation, evaluation and report. Maintain the documentation as you work.

The completion review will take place at the end of Sprint III. Follow the confirmed course announcements for the exact review, submission and final presentation dates.

### **By the End of This Sprint, I Expect to See**

* **Completed functionality linked to the objectives**, with a traceability record connecting each objective or requirement to its implemented component, test or evaluation, result and supporting evidence. Explain any unmet requirement and its effect honestly.  
* **A coherent system designed around real user tasks**, with suitable navigation, readable interfaces, consistent interactions, appropriate access controls and helpful feedback. Complete and verify each module before progressing to the next, then test the integrated workflows.
